title: The colossal cosmic eye NGC 1350
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1350, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
celestial: NGC 1350 · constellation Fornax · about 65 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: The spiral galaxy NGC 1350 looks like a gigantic eye in this color picture from the FORS2 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope. Delicate structures show clearly within it, and many more distant galaxies appear in the background.

The picture comes from just 16 minutes of observations in total, combined into one color composite. Color composites like this are made by combining separate exposures taken through different filters, each one assigned its own color.

A spiral galaxy is a flat, rotating disc of stars, gas and dust in which bright arms curl out from the center. NGC 1350 is about 65 million light-years away. The faint background galaxies scattered around it lie far beyond it and appear small because of their great distance.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (8.14 x 4.97 arcminutes) and distance (65 million light years), the frame spans roughly 154,000 × 94,000 light-years. Its light set out about 65 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The FORS2 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope recorded NGC 1350 through B, V, R and I filters, in visible and near-infrared light. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared filter records light the eye cannot see, and the galaxy is far too faint for the unaided eye.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: FORS2 observed the galaxy through four filters, three in visible light (B, V and R) and one in the near-infrared (I). The picture is credited to ESO. The galaxy lies in the constellation Fornax.
alt: A spiral galaxy shaped like a giant eye, with many small background galaxies around it.
